story: The Allies invaded Sicily on 10 July 1943 and the Italian mainland in September. Mussolini fell, Italy changed sides, and Germany occupied the peninsula, including Rome. Field Marshal Kesselring then fought a slow defensive war along a series of fortified lines across the mountains. The strongest, the Gustav Line, was anchored on Monte Cassino, which blocked Highway 6, the inland road to Rome. Four battles were fought there between January and May 1944, while an Allied landing at Anzio on 22 January, meant to outflank the line, was itself hemmed in for four months. Only in May, with Operation Diadem, did the Gustav Line break: French colonial troops crossed the mountains, Polish II Corps took the abbey heights and VI Corps broke out of the Anzio beachhead. US Fifth Army entered Rome on 4 June 1944, two days before D-Day. In occupied Rome, the German security police jailed and tortured opponents in Via Tasso and carried out the Ardeatine Caves massacre. Italy tied down large German forces, but it was a costly, grinding campaign that lasted until May 1945.

stops.name: Abbey of Monte Cassino
stops.text: The Benedictine abbey on Monte Cassino looks down on Highway 6 and the Liri valley, the inland route to Rome and the hinge of the German Gustav Line. Four Allied offensives were fought below it between January and May 1944. On 15 February Allied bombers destroyed the abbey, killing about 230 Italian civilians sheltering inside. German paratroopers then occupied the ruins and made them a strongpoint. The New Zealand Corps, including 4th Indian Division, failed to take Monastery Hill in February and March. In Operation Diadem, Polish II Corps attacked the heights and on 18 May a Polish cavalry patrol raised its flag over the ruins. The abbey was rebuilt and Pope Paul VI consecrated the new basilica on 24 October 1964.
stops.look: A complete, rebuilt abbey on the summit, reached by a winding road. From the terraces you look down on the Polish cemetery, Cassino town, the Rapido valley and Highway 6, and can see why the hill dominated the battle. Look for photographs of the ruins and the abbey museum.
stops.plan: Summer (1 Apr–31 Oct) open daily 9:30–18:30; winter Mon–Sat 9:30–16:15, Sundays and holidays 9:30–17:15. A working monastery: dress modestly and keep quiet during services. Museum and guided visits by arrangement; check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Whether German troops were in the abbey before the bombing is long disputed. Some Allied observers claimed they were, but the Germans had agreed with the Vatican not to occupy it, and the British official history and a 1969 US Army review concluded they made no military use of it before 15 February.

aar.ev: Allied bombers destroy the abbey; German paratroopers turn the ruins into a fortress.
aar.st: Four Allied offensives were fought below the abbey between January and May 1944. After bombers destroyed it on 15 February, German paratroopers held the ruins against the New Zealand Corps, until a Polish patrol raised its flag there on 18 May. Today a rebuilt abbey crowns the hill, and its terraces look down on the Polish cemetery, Cassino town and Highway 6.

q.t: What did German paratroopers do after the abbey was bombed?
o: Occupied the ruins and made them a strongpoint
Handed the site to the Vatican
q.x: The bombing did not clear the hill. German paratroopers moved into the ruins and used them as a strongpoint until Polish II Corps took the heights in May 1944.

aar.rem: Bombing the abbey gave the defenders better cover in the rubble than the intact building would have.

stops.notes: Price for the abbey museum not confirmed on the official site; the abbey phone is +39 0776 311529. About 9 km of hairpin road from Cassino town.

stops.name: Polish War Cemetery, Monte Cassino
stops.text: Polish II Corps under General Władysław Anders attacked the heights north-west of the abbey in May 1944, during Operation Diadem. After a week of fighting on Point 593 and the surrounding ridges, a patrol raised the Polish flag over the abbey ruins on 18 May. The cemetery lies on the slopes of Point 445, the Allied cemetery closest to the abbey. It was designed by Wacław Hryniewicz and Jerzy Skolimowski and consecrated on 1 September 1945. Crosses mark Christian graves and Stars of David mark Jewish ones. Anders, who died in London in 1970, chose to be buried among his men. A Memorial Museum on the 2nd Corps opened nearby in 2014.
stops.look: Terraced rows of travertine crosses rise to a large stone memorial, with the abbey directly above. Read the Simonides-style inscription ('Passer-by, go tell Poland...') and find General Anders' grave at the front. The small museum shows uniforms, photographs and film.
stops.plan: Free. Reached by the abbey road with parking nearby. Opening hours of the cemetery and the Memorial Museum could not be confirmed on an official site; check before you go and allow time if visiting with the abbey.
stops.disputed: Sources give different totals: Wikipedia states 1,072 Polish graves, while Italy's official tourism site counts 1,051 crosses.

aar.ev: A Polish patrol raises its flag over the abbey ruins after a week of fighting.
aar.st: Polish II Corps under General Anders attacked the ridges north-west of the abbey during Operation Diadem in May 1944. On 18 May a patrol raised the Polish flag over the ruins. The cemetery, consecrated in 1945, holds Anders himself among his men. Today terraced rows of crosses climb towards a stone memorial, with the rebuilt abbey directly above.
aar.rem: General Anders died in London in 1970 but chose to be buried here with his soldiers.

stops.notes: Grave count differs between sources (1,072 vs 1,051); avoid quoting an exact figure in the app or give both.

stops.name: Cassino War Cemetery and Memorial (CWGC)
stops.text: This Commonwealth cemetery lies on the valley floor below Monte Cassino, among the ground where British, Indian, New Zealand, Canadian and other Commonwealth troops fought between January and May 1944. It holds 4,271 Commonwealth servicemen, 289 of them unidentified. Inside the cemetery stands the Cassino Memorial, which carries the names of more than 4,000 Commonwealth servicemen who died in the Italian campaign and have no known grave. The New Zealand Corps attacks of February and March 1944 and the Eighth Army's crossing of the Rapido (Gari) in May were fought within sight of this spot.
stops.look: Rows of headstones in a walled garden, with the abbey on its hill above. The Cassino Memorial is a series of green marble panels around a pool. Look up from the cemetery to Monastery Hill to see the slopes the infantry had to climb.
stops.plan: Free. CWGC sites are normally open access; check the CWGC website for any works before you go. Short drive from Cassino town centre.

aar.ev: Commonwealth dead of the four Cassino battles are gathered beneath Monastery Hill.
aar.st: This cemetery lies on the valley floor where Commonwealth troops fought between January and May 1944. It holds 4,271 servicemen, and the Cassino Memorial inside names more than 4,000 more who have no known grave. Today rows of headstones fill a walled garden, with green marble memorial panels around a pool and the abbey on its hill above.
aar.rem: Look up from the headstones to Monastery Hill to understand the ground these men attacked.

stops.notes: The CWGC page could not be fetched (error); coordinates are from Wikipedia and only have 4 decimals. Verify on the CWGC page and exact gate position before publication.

stops.name: German War Cemetery, Cassino (Caira)
stops.text: About 3 km north of Cassino, on the southern foothills of Colle Marino, lies the largest German war cemetery in Italy. In 1959–1960 the Volksbund moved 20,076 German dead here from smaller cemeteries and field graves across the region, including the men who held the Gustav Line around Cassino and those who fought on the Garigliano and in the mountains. Around 3,100 graves have no name. The cemetery opened on 4 May 1965. In 2014 seven plaques were added in the memorial hall for 911 unidentified dead.
stops.look: Terraces and ellipses of graves climb the hillside, marked by stone crosses carrying several names each. The open-roofed, cube-shaped entrance building lights the sculpture 'Mourning and Consolation' by Suse Müller-Diefenbach. There is a small exhibition and wide views towards Monte Cassino.
stops.plan: Free. Summer: Mon–Fri 9:00–18:00, weekends and holidays 9:00–19:00; winter: daily 8:00–16:00. Parking at Piazza Marino Fardelli, Caira. Accessible. Check the Volksbund page before you go.

aar.ev: German dead from across the Cassino front are brought together on Colle Marino.
aar.st: In 1959–1960 the Volksbund moved more than 20,000 German dead here from smaller cemeteries and field graves, including the defenders of the Gustav Line. The cemetery opened on 4 May 1965, and thousands of its graves carry no name. Today terraces of stone crosses climb the hillside from an open-roofed entrance hall with a sculpture of mourning and consolation.
aar.rem: Many of the men buried here held the same ridges the Allied dead in the valley below were trying to take.

stops.notes: Volksbund gives both 'Via Colle Marino 1' and '2' as the address.

stops.name: Anzio Beachhead Museum (Museo dello Sbarco)
stops.text: On 22 January 1944 US VI Corps under Major General John P. Lucas landed at Anzio and Nettuno in Operation Shingle, to outflank the Gustav Line. US 3rd Infantry Division came ashore at X-Ray beach, British 1st Infantry Division at Peter beach and US Rangers took the port. Lucas consolidated rather than drive inland, and General von Mackensen's Fourteenth Army sealed the beachhead. Major General Lucian Truscott replaced Lucas on 22 February. The breakout, Operation Buffalo, began on 23 May, and Rome fell on 4 June. The museum was founded on 22 January 1994, the 50th anniversary, by a local research association.
stops.look: A single room in the 17th-century Villa Adele, organised in American, British, German and Italian sections: uniforms, weapons, maps, documents and veterans' photographs. Look for objects raised from the seabed off Anzio, including from HMS Janus, HMS Spartan and the hospital ship St David.
stops.plan: Open Tue and Thu–Sun 10:00–13:00 and 16:00–18:00; closed Mon and Wed. July–August 10:00–13:00 and 17:00–19:00. No booking needed. Short walk from Anzio station; check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Mark Clark's decision on 25–26 May to turn north-west for Rome rather than cut Route 6 at Valmontone is still argued over; Truscott and others held that it let much of the German Tenth Army escape.
links: Museo dello Sbarco di Anzio (Ministero della Cultura)

aar.ev: US VI Corps lands at Anzio to outflank the Gustav Line, then is boxed in.
aar.st: On 22 January 1944 US VI Corps under Lucas landed at Anzio and Nettuno. Lucas consolidated instead of driving inland, and German Fourteenth Army sealed the beachhead for four months until the breakout of 23 May. Today a room in the 17th-century Villa Adele holds uniforms, weapons, maps and objects raised from ships sunk off Anzio.

q.t: Who replaced Major General Lucas in command of VI Corps at Anzio in February 1944?
q.x: Truscott, who had led US 3rd Infantry Division ashore, replaced Lucas on 22 February 1944 and commanded the May breakout.

aar.rem: Anzio was meant to unlock Cassino; instead it needed Cassino's fall to break out.

stops.notes: Admission price not stated on official pages seen. Museum is small; combine with the Beachhead and the Nettuno cemetery. Coordinates from TracesOfWar, not the museum.

stops.name: Sicily-Rome American Cemetery, Nettuno
stops.text: On the northern edge of Nettuno, inside the old Anzio beachhead, the American Battle Monuments Commission cemetery holds 7,858 American war dead on 77 acres. Most died in the campaigns from the landing in Sicily on 10 July 1943, through Salerno and the winter fighting, to the Anzio beachhead and the advance on Rome in June 1944. The white marble walls of the chapel carry 3,095 names of the missing. The memorial was designed by Murphy & Locraft and the grounds by Allyn R. Jennings; the cemetery was dedicated in 1956.
stops.look: Long curving rows of marble crosses and Stars of David on a lawn framed by Roman pines, leading to the chapel and the Tablets of the Missing. The memorial building has large maps of the Sicily and Italian campaigns. Staff in the visitor building can help find a grave.
stops.plan: Free; no booking. Open daily 9:00–17:00 (last entry 16:45), closed 25 December and 1 January. Piazzale Kennedy 1, Nettuno. Check the ABMC website before you go.

aar.ev: Americans killed from Sicily to Rome are buried inside the old Anzio beachhead.
aar.st: This cemetery lies inside the ground held by VI Corps during the Anzio beachhead battles. It holds 7,858 American dead from the Sicily landing to the capture of Rome, and the chapel names 3,095 missing. Today long rows of marble headstones under Roman pines lead to a chapel and a memorial building with large campaign maps.
aar.rem: The cemetery stands inside the beachhead that Allied troops held for four months.

stops.notes: Wikipedia also mentions 7,861 headstones; 7,858 burials used here.

stops.name: Fosse Ardeatine Mausoleum, Rome
stops.text: On 23 March 1944 Communist-led GAP partisans bombed a column of the 11th Company, 3rd Battalion, SS Police Regiment 'Bozen' in Via Rasella; 33 policemen eventually died. Hitler authorised a reprisal of ten Italians for each German killed. Herbert Kappler, head of the security police in Rome, drew up the list, using prisoners, Jews and others; Erich Priebke and Karl Hass led the killing squads. On 24 March 335 men and boys, five more than ordered, were shot in disused quarries on the Via Ardeatina, and the tunnels were blown to hide the bodies. The mausoleum, the result of a national competition, was inaugurated on 24 March 1949.
stops.look: You enter through a gate with bronze sculpture, then walk through the tunnels where the shooting took place. The mausoleum is a vast, low concrete slab over 335 identical tombs, plus one for all Italy's fallen of the liberation war. A small museum explains the events.
stops.plan: Mon–Fri 8:15–15:15, Sat–Sun 8:15–16:45. Entry has traditionally been free. Guided visits through ANFIM (info@anfim.org). Via Ardeatina 174, near the Appian Way catacombs. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: How much the Vatican knew in advance is debated: a Vatican note on the morning of 24 March expected a ten-for-one reprisal, and historians such as Robert Katz have argued Pius XII did too little, which his defenders reject.

aar.ev: German security police shoot 335 Roman prisoners and civilians in the Ardeatine quarries.
aar.st: After partisans bombed a German police column in Via Rasella on 23 March 1944, Hitler authorised a ten-for-one reprisal. Herbert Kappler's security police shot 335 men and boys in quarries on the Via Ardeatina the next day and blew the tunnels shut. Today you walk through the tunnels to a vast concrete mausoleum sheltering 335 identical tombs.
aar.rem: The reprisal was ordered at ten for one, and five more men were killed than even that order demanded.

stops.notes: Admission price not stated on the official site (traditionally free). Coordinates from Rome's official tourism site.

stops.name: Museum of the Liberation of Rome (Via Tasso)
stops.text: This late-1930s apartment block near St John Lateran was first rented to the German embassy. After the Germans took Rome in September 1943, the SS security police and SD under Herbert Kappler made it their headquarters, with a prison at number 145. More than 2,000 anti-fascists, resisters and Jews passed through its cells; many were tortured, and some were later shot at Forte Bravetta or the Fosse Ardeatine. When the Germans fled in June 1944 they left some prisoners behind. Princess Josepha Ruspoli donated the flats to the state in 1950, and the museum opened on 4 June 1955.
stops.look: Small former cells on several floors, some kept with prisoners' scratched graffiti on the walls. Displays cover the occupation, the round-up of Rome's Jews, the Resistance and the Ardeatine massacre, with documents, photographs and personal objects.
stops.plan: Open daily 9:00–19:00, including Sundays and holidays; closed some holidays and 14–16 August. Free (voluntary donation). Booking required only for groups over six. Free guided visit first Sunday of the month at 10:30. Metro Manzoni.
links: Museum of the Liberation of Rome (Wikipedia)

aar.ev: Kappler's SS security police turn an apartment block into a prison and interrogation centre.
aar.st: From September 1943 the SS security police under Herbert Kappler ran their headquarters and prison here. More than 2,000 people passed through its cells, many of them tortured, and some later died at the Fosse Ardeatine. Today the former cells hold displays on the occupation and Resistance, and some walls still carry prisoners' graffiti.
aar.rem: Victims of the Fosse Ardeatine were taken from these cells.

stops.notes: Treated as solemn (former prison and torture site).

stops.name: Sicily Landing Museum 1943, Catania
stops.text: Operation Husky began on the night of 9/10 July 1943 with airborne drops and landings at 02:45 on 10 July: Patton's US Seventh Army in the south-west and Montgomery's British Eighth Army in the south-east. British airborne troops seized the Ponte Grande bridge near Syracuse and fought for Primosole Bridge south of Catania, where the Eighth Army's advance was held up below Etna. Mussolini's regime fell during the campaign. US 3rd Division entered Messina on the night of 16 August and the campaign ended on 17 August, but over 100,000 German and Italian troops escaped across the Straits. The museum, opened in December 2002, tells the story of the campaign.
stops.look: Three floors of a converted sulphur works at Le Ciminiere. A mock-up Sicilian piazza leads into a dark air-raid shelter with a simulated bombing, then out to a ruined square. Uniforms and weapons of all sides, an Italian bunker, wax figures and guns outside.
stops.plan: Daily 9:00–19:00, last entry 18:00. Adults €8, reduced €4; combined tickets with other Ciminiere museums. No booking needed. Paid parking nearby is checked frequently. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Figures for the Axis evacuation across the Straits of Messina differ: about 52,000 Germans and 62,000 Italians in British-based accounts, 60,000 Germans by the OKW's count and about 75,000 Italians in Italian figures.
links: Museo Storico dello Sbarco in Sicilia 1943 (Ministero della Cultura)

aar.ev: Patton's and Montgomery's armies land in Sicily, opening the campaign in Italy.
aar.st: Operation Husky began with airborne drops and landings on 10 July 1943, Patton's Seventh Army in the south-west and Montgomery's Eighth Army in the south-east. Messina fell on 17 August, but over 100,000 Axis troops escaped to the mainland. Today a converted sulphur works holds a mock Sicilian piazza, a simulated air-raid shelter and weapons and uniforms of all sides.

q.t: Which Allied commander's army landed in south-eastern Sicily?
q.x: Montgomery's British Eighth Army landed in the south-east and pushed up the east coast towards Catania; Patton's US Seventh Army landed in the south-west.

aar.rem: Sicily was taken in 38 days, but most of the Axis garrison got away to fight again in Italy.

stops.notes: ADDED STOP (Italy campaign starts in Sicily). Address given as Viale Africa (Le Ciminiere) by the Ministry and Via Vittorio Emanuele II 201 by TracesOfWar; coordinates from TracesOfWar, verify the entrance. Opening date of Dec 2002 from the Ministry page.
